Stage 3 · Grammar

How to complain and still be welcome

The complaint is the easy part. English does the work in the words around it.

Read these four pairs. The left one and the right one say the same thing.
  • Bring me a cloth.  →  Could you possibly bring me a cloth?
  • There is a mistake in the bill.  →  There seems to be a mistake in the bill.
  • I can’t eat this.  →  I’m afraid I can’t eat this.
  • Wait while I get some money.  →  Would you mind waiting while I get some money?
What do the four phrases on the right all do?
The four jobs, and the phrases that do them
The jobWhat you sayNote
Open itExcuse me. · Excuse me, I’m very sorry, but…never start with the problem itself
Soften the problemThere seems to be a mistake… · I’m afraid I can’t eat this… · I’ve got a bit of a problem.seems to be = “I am not accusing anyone”
Ask for the fixCould you possibly bring me…? · Could I have another glass, please? · Would you mind waiting…?after would you mind → -ing recycled
Say what is wrongIt’s dirty. · It smells funny. · You’ve charged us for two coffees. · My fish was overcooked. passivethe passive keeps blame off the person
The waiter repliesI’m terribly sorry. · I do apologize. · Don’t worry, it’s not your fault. · I’ll get you another one.I do apologize is the most formal
Now soften each direct sentence. Type the missing words.
1Bring me a clean glass. → Could I another glass, please?
2There is a mistake in the bill. → There a mistake in the bill.
3I can’t eat this fish. → I’m I can’t eat this fish.
4Wait five minutes. → Would you five minutes?
5Bring me a cloth. → Could you me a cloth?

THE SHAPE. Open (Excuse me) → soften (I’m afraid… / There seems to be…) → say what is wrong → ask for the fix (Could you possibly…?).

THE PASSIVE HELPS. My fish was overcooked is a complaint about the fish. You overcooked my fish is a complaint about the cook.

Not “Bring me a cloth”, not “Would you mind to wait”, not “You are wrong in the bill”.

The same softening comes back in Unit 11 for disagreeing politely: I’m afraid I disagree.

THE SHAPE. A complaint in English has four moves and they always run in this order: open (Excuse me.) → soften (I’m very sorry, but… / I’m afraid… / There seems to be…) → say what is wrong → ask for the fix (Could you possibly…? Could I have…?). Skip the first two and a perfectly reasonable complaint sounds like an attack.

WHY SEEMS. There seems to be a mistake does not mean you are unsure. It means you are giving the other person a way out. English does this constantly, and leaving it out is the single biggest reason polite learners sound rude.

WOULD YOU MIND IS THE TRAP. It is followed by the -ing form: Would you mind waiting? And the answer is upside down — Not at all means yes, that is fine.

THE PASSIVE DOES THE DIPLOMACY. recycled My fish was overcooked talks about the fish. You overcooked my fish talks about the cook. In a restaurant, and in a written review, you almost always want the first one.

WHAT THE WAITER SAYS BACK. I’m terribly sorry · I do apologize (the most formal) · Don’t worry, it’s not your fault · I’ll get you another one. You will need these when you take the waiter’s card in the role play.

The three mistakes to watch: a bare imperative (“Bring me a cloth”) · Would you mind to wait · blaming the person instead of the food.

The same softeners return in Unit 11 for disagreeing politely: I’m afraid I disagree. I’m not so sure.

Five phrases from the recording. Press Listen and copy the intonation in your head, not out loud.

Full grammar reference — Complaining politely in a restaurant

Form

Getting attentionExcuse me…
The problemThere’s a problem with my order. · This isn’t what I ordered.
Being specificThe soup is cold. · The meat is overcooked.
The requestCould you change it, please? · Would it be possible to have another one?
PayingCould we have the bill, please?

When and why we use it

  • Softeners do the work: I’m sorry, but…, I’m afraid…, Excuse me…
  • Describe the problem factually, then ask for one clear thing.
  • Use could, not can or the imperative.
  • In a written review the same information is arranged differently: what was good first, then the problem, then whether you recommend it.

Signal words

Excuse me · I’m afraid · a bit · rather · actually

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Bring me another one. → Could you bring me another one, please?An imperative sounds rude to a stranger.
  • This food is disgusting. → I’m afraid this isn’t what I ordered.Describe, do not attack.
  • There is a problem in my order. → There is a problem with my order.Problem with.
  • Give me the bill. → Could we have the bill, please?Standard polite form.

Don’t confuse it with

I’m afraid is not fear. It simply warns the listener that something unwelcome is coming.

Stage 6 · ★ model

The model review

The meal was last night. This is what she wrote about it this morning. Read it as a writer.

Kara Balyq — worth the wait, but only just

Aliya K. · posted on a restaurant site · ★★★★☆

We went to Kara Balyq on Saturday for my sister’s birthday, and I have been thinking about it ever since — for two different reasons.

The good part. The atmosphere is the best thing here. The room is small, the light is low, and the bread is baked in front of you. Our starters were excellent: the aubergines are grilled over a fire and served with a thick, slightly sour sauce, and the portions are generous. For 6,000 tenge a head it is very good value.

The problem. My sister ordered the sea bass. When it came, it was badly overcooked — dry all the way through. We told the waiter, who apologised immediately, and a new one was brought within ten minutes. The second fish was perfect. But we then waited almost half an hour for the bill, and nobody came when we asked. The only downside was the service at the end of the evening; everything before that was excellent.

Would I go back? Yes. I would recommend it for a small group rather than a large one, and I would ask for the bill before you think you need it. Book a table — it was full by nine.

Note. Written for this course as a writing model. The restaurant and the reviewer are invented.

The role play, then the review

Useful language

Customer: Excuse me… · I’m very sorry, but… · There seems to be a problem with… · This isn’t what I ordered. · I’m afraid I can’t eat this. · Could you possibly…? · Could we have the bill? · Would you mind waiting…?

Waiter: I’m terribly sorry. · I do apologize. · Don’t worry, it’s not your fault. · I’ll get you another one. · That’s no problem.

Review: The atmosphere is… · The portions are… · It is very good value. · The only downside was… · I would recommend it for…

1 · Work in pairs. Take one card each. Do not show it.

You each know your own goal only. Open, soften, say the problem, ask for the fix.

Card A — customer

You ordered lamb; they brought chicken. You have been waiting fifty minutes and you have a train in forty. You want the right dish or no charge for it. Be polite — you like this place.

Card B — waiter

The kitchen is short-staffed tonight. You can offer a free dessert or take the dish off the bill, but you cannot cook a new main course in under twenty minutes. Apologise properly.

Run the conversation. It should last about two minutes.
2 · Swap roles and take the second pair of cards.
Card C — customer

The bill has two extra sparkling waters on it, and your portion was tiny. You do not have enough cash and they do not take cards. Sort both problems out.

Card D — waiter

The waters were for the table next to them — your mistake. There is a cash machine four minutes away. You cannot let a customer leave without paying, but you can offer to wait.

Run it again with the second card. This run is the one that matters.
